label: Person
name: Sírlám
summary:
Sírlám, son of Finn mac Blatha, was, according to medieval Irish legend and historical tradition, a High King of Ireland. He took power after killing his predecessor Lugaid Íardonn in battle at Ráith Clochair. His name means 'long hand' or 'long arm' in Old Irish, and it is said his arms reached to his ankles — a supernatural physical characteristic that in Irish tradition often marks a figure of exceptional power or magical origin.

Like Lugaid Íardonn and Fíachu Findoilches, Sírlám belongs to the deep layer of legendary Irish High Kings whose stories were assembled by monastic scholars in the 8th–10th centuries CE to provide Ireland with a continuous pre-Christian regal history. The violent succession pattern — killing one's predecessor — is a recurring feature of this mythological stratum and may reflect archaic ritual or simply the literary conventions of the genre.

Sírlám's supernatural physical description (arms reaching to the ankles) connects him to a broader Indo-European mythological tradition of heroic figures distinguished by anomalous body proportions. In Irish tradition, such figures often belong to the Otherworld or are associated with druidic power. His story was preserved in the Lebor Gabála Érenn and various annalistic compilations as part of the grand synthetic project of Irish historical mythology that gave later dynasties their legitimating ancestry.
